title: After you're gone
hookLine: Honi meets a man planting a carob tree that won't fruit for seventy years
tomorrow: what did Thoreau say when asked to make his peace with God?

cards: Carob tastes like chocolate that grew up on a farm: sweet, a little dusty, eaten straight from a long brown pod. The Talmud tells a story about a carob tree.
Honi, a holy man known as the Circle-Drawer, is walking along a road and sees a man planting one. How long until it bears fruit? Honi asks.
Seventy years, says the man. And you're sure you'll live seventy years? The man answers: I found the world full of carob trees.
My ancestors planted them for me. So I'm planting these for my children.

teach.b: Then the story turns. Honi sits down to eat, sleep comes over him, a rock grows up around him, and he sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, a man is gathering carobs from that very tree.
Did you plant this? Honi asks. No, says the man.
I'm his grandson. The planter is gone. The fruit isn't.

teach.h: A LINE: PLANTED FOR, PLANTING FOR.
teach.b: That's a Jewish teaching, and this path borrows it with its name on: you stand in a line, between the people who planted for you and the people you'll plant for. The rabbis push it further.

A saying attributed to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai goes: if you're holding a sapling and someone shouts that the Messiah has come, plant the sapling first, then go out to greet him. The planting matters that much.

So after you're gone isn't only a question about where you'll be. It's about what you're putting in the ground now: a tree, a recipe a kid will cook one day, a kindness someone learned by watching you.
You won't taste most of it. It's still yours.

how: Jewish tradition tells Honi's story to teach planting for the next generation; people who borrow it plant a tree, teach a recipe, or start something they won't see finished.

o: the paperwork a family sorts out after a death
what happens to the soul once someone dies
what you leave for the people who come after you

games.q: the carob story: tap the pairs.
p: asked: will you live to eat it?
plant it first, then greet the Messiah

s: the carob planter expected to eat the fruit himself
he planted for his children, as his ancestors had planted for him.
in the story, Honi sleeps for seventy years
he wakes to find the planter's grandson gathering carobs from that tree.
leaving something behind mostly means being remembered
the popular version. in Honi's story, the planter isn't named; the tree is what's left, feeding a grandson.

games.q: a coworker is retiring and wonders if it's worth training the new hire, since she won't see the results. what fits Honi's story?
o: train him: others trained her, so she trains those after. the fruit isn't hers to eat.
train him only in what pays off before she leaves; the rest is wasted effort.
skip it: the new hire should figure it out alone, the way she had to.
games.why: the planter found the world full of trees his ancestors planted, so he planted for his children. Honi slept seventy years and woke to a grandson eating the fruit.

practice: Hold something that grew: a seed, a leaf from a plant, a piece of fruit, or a pinch of soil. Feel its weight and its texture as you breathe.
Then name, silently, one person who planted something you're still eating from, and one thing you might plant for after.

wordCard.voice: After you're gone: what you plant now that others will eat from later, the way Honi's planter fed a grandson he may never have met.

orig.note: Hebrew: carob, the tree in Honi's story (Talmud, Taanit 23a).

carryVoice: Carry this: for after, a tree whose fruit you may never taste. Six of seven, see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a (Honi and the man planting a carob; the seventy-year sleep; the grandson)
Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version B, ch. 31 (if you are holding a sapling when they say the Messiah has come, plant it first)
